blocks.text: An instruction dataset is a collection of examples structured around a task instruction, an optional piece of input context, and the expected output, the format that turns a raw pretrained model into one that reliably follows directions.

This is one of the most widely used dataset shapes in fine-tuning today, and getting its structure right, clear instructions, appropriately included input, and correct outputs, has an outsized effect on how well the resulting model follows real world instructions.
1. What an Instruction Dataset Actually Is

blocks.alt: An instruction, an optional input, and an expected output form one instruction example

blocks.text: Each example in an instruction dataset represents one task, described through a natural language instruction, optionally paired with additional input the task needs, and always paired with the correct output the model should learn to produce.
This structure directly extends the instruction fine-tuning idea introduced earlier in the Types of Fine-Tuning topic, this topic focuses specifically on how to build the dataset itself.
2. Writing a Good Instruction Field

blocks.alt: A vague instruction is compared against a clear, specific one

blocks.text: A vague instruction, like improve this text, teaches the model an ambiguous notion of the task, while a specific instruction, like rewrite this text in a more formal tone while keeping it under fifty words, gives the model a much clearer signal about exactly what output is expected.
The clarity of the instruction field during training directly shapes how well the fine-tuned model handles similarly phrased instructions at inference time.
3. When the Input Field Is Optional

blocks.alt: A task needing extra context includes an input field, otherwise it is omitted

blocks.text: Some tasks are fully self contained in the instruction, write a haiku about autumn, needs no separate input. Others genuinely require additional context, summarize this document, needs the document itself supplied as a separate input field.
Keeping this distinction clean, rather than always cramming everything into the instruction text, makes the dataset easier to reason about and format consistently.

blocks.text: 4. Instruction Diversity, Why It Matters

blocks.alt: A narrow instruction variety is compared against a diverse instruction variety

blocks.text: A dataset built from only a handful of instruction phrasings teaches a model to follow those specific phrasings well, but it may struggle with the same underlying task phrased differently at inference time.

Deliberately varying how instructions are worded across the dataset, while keeping the underlying task consistent, tends to produce a model that generalizes better to the many different ways real users actually phrase requests.

blocks.title: Diversity in phrasing, not just in task
blocks.content: A dataset can cover many different tasks and still lack diversity if every instruction for a given task type is phrased almost identically, both kinds of diversity matter.

blocks.text: 5. Instruction Datasets vs Chat Datasets

blocks.alt: An instruction dataset built for single turn tasks is compared against a chat dataset built for multi-turn conversation

blocks.text: Instruction datasets are typically single turn, one instruction, one response, well suited to task oriented fine-tuning like summarization, classification, or extraction.

Chat datasets, covered in the next topic of this module, extend this idea across multiple turns of back and forth conversation, which matters when the deployed model needs to hold a genuine dialogue rather than answer isolated one off requests.
6. Sourcing Instructions, Hand Written vs Synthetic

blocks.alt: Hand written instructions are compared against synthetically generated ones

blocks.text: Instructions can be written by hand, giving high control over quality and phrasing at the cost of speed, or generated synthetically using the techniques covered in the earlier Synthetic Data Generation topic, trading some control for much faster scale.
Most real instruction datasets blend both, hand written examples anchoring quality, synthetic examples expanding coverage and volume.

8. Structuring Examples for Different Task Types

The same three field structure adapts naturally across very different task types, classification, extraction, generation, and rewriting, since the instruction field simply describes whatever task is at hand while the input and output fields carry the task specific content.
9. Common Structural Pitfalls

blocks.alt: An output that does not actually match its instruction confuses the training signal

blocks.text: The most damaging structural mistake is an output that does not genuinely match its paired instruction, whether from a copy paste error during dataset assembly or a mislabeled example that slipped through cleaning, since the model has no way to detect this inconsistency and simply learns from it as if it were correct.
Worked Example

A team building a fine-tuned model for internal documentation tasks collects three thousand instruction examples covering summarizing, rewriting, and extracting key points from documents, deliberately varying the phrasing of each instruction type across the dataset, rewrite this, please make this more concise, shorten the following, all appearing for the same underlying rewriting task.

After training, they find the model handles a wide range of naturally phrased user requests well, a direct result of the phrasing diversity built into the dataset rather than relying on one rigid instruction template.
Common Mistakes

items: Writing instructions so vague that the correct output is genuinely ambiguous
Cramming context into the instruction field instead of using a separate input field when the task requires it
Using the same handful of instruction phrasings for every example of a given task type
Letting an output slip through that does not actually match its paired instruction

blocks.text: Practice

Take one task you want a model to perform and write five different instruction phrasings for it, all describing the same underlying task but worded the way five different real users might naturally phrase the request.
Key Takeaway

An instruction dataset structures training examples around a clear instruction, an appropriately included input, and a correct output, and diversifying instruction phrasing while keeping outputs genuinely correct is what determines how well the resulting fine-tuned model follows real, naturally worded requests.
